methodological_rigor.justification: Matched retrospective cohort study with adequate design but identifiable limitations. Sequential matching by age and diagnosis year strengthens comparability. Appropriate statistical methods include Kaplan-Meier, Cox regression, and Log-rank tests with proper reporting. However, the study lacks prospective data, retains selection bias inherent to retrospective design, and admits missing data on comorbidities and socioeconomic factors. Small sample size (n=57 per group) and single geographic region limit generalizability despite universal healthcare access.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Individual matched cohort study directly investigating clinical utility of surveillance in smoldering myeloma. The comparison of myeloma-defining events and survival between monitored and unmonitored cohorts has direct clinical relevance for patient management decisions. Findings suggest surveillance effectiveness in reducing end-organ damage and improving outcomes. As a retrospective matched cohort, this maps to LoE 2b per Oxford CEBM. Results inform clinical practice regarding surveillance benefits and limitations.

reporting_quality.justification: Manuscript follows observational study reporting conventions with clear methods section, definitions of endpoints, and results tables. However, gaps include: no mention of pre-registration or protocol publication, limited discussion of missing data frequency and mechanisms, no explicit data availability or sharing statement, and undefined local institutional review board approval details. These omissions limit transparency and reproducibility.

novelty_literature.justification: The study presents a meaningful clinical contribution by comparing disease burden and outcomes in monitored SMM progression versus de novo presentation. While surveillance benefit has been previously hypothesized, this study rigorously quantifies advantages (44% vs. 72% irreversible damage, 59% vs. 30% 3-year PFS). The work extends prior smaller studies (e.g., Goyal et al. 2019, Go et al. 2015) with contemporary data and detailed organ-damage assessment, representing incremental but clinically meaningful extension of knowledge.

writing_presentation.justification: Well-organized manuscript with clear introduction establishing SMM clinical context, systematic methods, and comprehensive results tables. The discussion thoughtfully contextualizes findings within existing literature and acknowledges limitations transparently. Strengths include explicit discussion of lead-time bias, biological heterogeneity, and comparison with AQUILA trial findings. Minor areas for improvement include some redundancy in results restatement, but overall publication-ready quality is evident.

key_strengths: Rigorous matched-cohort design with sequential matching by age and diagnosis year improving comparability
Clinically meaningful primary outcomes (irreversible end-organ damage, 3-year PFS/OS) demonstrating surveillance benefit
Transparent acknowledgment of limitations including potential lead-time bias, biological heterogeneity, and missing socioeconomic data
Clear comparison to AQUILA trial and discussion of implications for evolving SMM treatment paradigm
key_concerns: Retrospective design with inherent selection bias; prospective validation needed to confirm surveillance efficacy
Missing data on comorbidities and socioeconomic factors limits ability to assess confounding despite age-matching
Single geographic region in Israel limits generalizability despite universal healthcare access
Small sample size (n=57 per arm) and acknowledgment that lead-time bias may explain part of survival advantage
No pre-registration or protocol publication limiting transparency
chief_reviewer.rationale: Well-conducted matched-cohort study demonstrating that SMM surveillance is associated with lower disease burden, fewer irreversible complications, and improved survival compared to de novo myeloma. Appropriate methodology and clinically meaningful outcomes support tier-3 journal placement. Retrospective design and potential lead-time bias require acknowledgment but do not negate value for clinical practice planning.
